messages.content: I want to design a GPU-sharing runtime that bounds inference latency while reclaiming memory from concurrent, stateful training jobs. The requirements are that, under admitted mixed workloads, inference p99 latency stays within 1.2× its isolated baseline, and training maintains forward progress through memory reclamation without restarting or corrupting optimizer state.

That gives the runtime two simultaneous obligations. It must protect the inference tail-latency bound when inference and training share the GPU, while making memory used by the concurrent training jobs reclaimable. Reclamation also has to preserve each training job’s ability to continue and the integrity of its optimizer state.
How should I read the 1.2× requirement? Is it about typical inference latency?

It is specifically about p99 latency, not an average or typical request. For an admitted mixed workload, inference p99 must be no greater than 1.2 times its isolated baseline. The comparison is to inference in isolation; the requirement does not say that every individual request must fall below that threshold.
So the latency condition applies whenever any combination of inference and training happens to run together?

The stated scope is **admitted mixed workloads**. It does not claim the bound for every conceivable combination of work, nor does it specify how admission is decided. The design needs to meet the p99 bound for the mixed workloads it admits.
What does “forward progress through memory reclamation” rule out?

It rules out treating reclamation as a reason to restart the training job or leave it unable to keep advancing. Reclaimed memory may belong to a stateful training job, so continuing must not come at the cost of corrupting its optimizer state. The requirement does not prescribe a particular reclamation mechanism or a numerical training-throughput target.
Does it require training to run without ever pausing?

Not as written. It requires forward progress *through* reclamation without a restart or optimizer-state corruption. That is distinct from promising that training never waits at any point. Any waiting, however, cannot turn reclamation into a permanent loss of progress.
Could the runtime satisfy the inference target by making training restart after it gives up memory?

No. The inference target and the training-continuity requirement both apply. A design that reaches the p99 target by restarting the stateful training jobs during reclamation would fail the stated training requirement.
And keeping training running is not enough if inference p99 exceeds the limit?

Right. Forward progress alone does not satisfy the goal. Under admitted mixed workloads, inference p99 still has to remain within 1.2× its isolated baseline. The runtime has to meet the latency condition and the reclamation-and-continuity condition together.
Is protecting optimizer state just another way of saying the job should not restart?

They are related but separate constraints. A job might continue without restarting yet have corrupted optimizer state; that would still violate the requirement. Conversely, preserving state does not make a restart acceptable. Training must maintain forward progress through reclamation, without either restarting or corrupting optimizer state.
What makes the training jobs’ being stateful important to the design goal?

It means reclaiming their memory cannot be considered only as freeing capacity. The runtime must also account for the fact that training has state that must remain valid as it proceeds—explicitly including optimizer state. The goal names that constraint but does not specify where the state resides or how reclamation preserves it.
Would an isolated inference result by itself show that the runtime meets the latency requirement?

No. The isolated result supplies the comparison baseline. The stated bound concerns inference p99 **under admitted mixed workloads**, while memory is reclaimed from concurrent, stateful training jobs. An isolated result alone would not establish how inference behaves under those mixed conditions.
Can you put the design objective in one sentence without adding a particular implementation?

Design a GPU-sharing runtime that, for admitted mixed workloads, keeps inference p99 latency at or below 1.2× its isolated baseline while reclaiming memory from concurrent, stateful training jobs that continue making forward progress without restarting or corrupting optimizer state.
What would you propose for the GPU-sharing runtime we just described?

I would combine four elements: latency-profiled admission, bounded training kernel slices, inference-priority dispatch, and versioned optimizer-state offload with asynchronous prefetch at step boundaries. Together, they address which mixed workloads are admitted, how long training can occupy the GPU before inference gets a dispatch opportunity, and how training can continue when optimizer-state memory is reclaimed. This is a proposed design, not a claim that it already meets the latency and training requirements.
Why start with latency-profiled admission rather than relying on scheduling alone?

The inference bound applies to admitted mixed workloads. Latency-profiled admission makes that condition an explicit part of the design: latency information informs which combinations the runtime accepts for sharing. Scheduling still matters after admission, but admission avoids treating the p99 target as a promise for arbitrary concurrent work. The proposal does not specify a profiling method or an admission rule.
Does “latency-profiled” mean the runtime has already demonstrated the 1.2× bound?

No. Using latency profiles to guide admission is a proposed mechanism, not evidence that inference p99 stays within 1.2× its isolated baseline. That bound remains a requirement to assess under the mixed workloads the runtime admits.
How do bounded training kernel slices fit with inference-priority dispatch?

Inference-priority dispatch gives inference preference when dispatch choices are made. Bounded training kernel slices limit how long a training slice can occupy the GPU before another such choice becomes possible. The two ideas complement each other: priority alone does not specify when the runtime next has an opportunity to act on it, while slices alone do not specify which work gets preference then.
Are you proposing that an inference request interrupts a training kernel immediately?

No immediate interruption is specified. The proposal is for bounded training kernel slices and inference-priority dispatch; it does not prescribe a preemption mechanism or say that inference can displace a kernel already running. Nor does it give a numerical slice bound.
Could priority for inference leave training stuck?

It cannot be allowed to defeat the separate requirement that training maintain forward progress through memory reclamation. “Inference-priority” describes a dispatch preference, not permission to abandon the training jobs. The proposal does not yet spell out a scheduling rule that resolves every possible contention pattern.
The memory side is less clear to me. What is being offloaded?

The proposal specifically names optimizer-state offload. That is the state it proposes to move out of GPU memory for reclamation, with versioning to distinguish the state that training must use as it continues. It does not specify an offload destination, which portions of the state are moved, or a storage format.
Why include versioning instead of just saying optimizer-state offload?

Because the training jobs are stateful and optimizer-state corruption is explicitly unacceptable. Versioning identifies which optimizer-state version an offloaded or prefetched piece belongs to, so the design can reason about preserving the right state as training advances. The word “versioned” expresses that intent; it does not, by itself, establish a complete correctness protocol.
And the asynchronous prefetch happens at step boundaries?

Yes—that is the timing named in the proposal. Asynchronous prefetch at step boundaries is paired with versioned optimizer-state offload so that reclaimed state can be brought back for training to continue. The proposal does not specify an exact trigger within a boundary, how much is prefetched, or a guarantee that prefetch always finishes without waiting.
Does reclaiming that memory require restarting the training job?

It must not. The proposed offload and prefetch are meant to support continued training through memory reclamation, consistent with the requirement not to restart or corrupt optimizer state. Whether a particular implementation achieves that still depends on preserving the necessary state correctly and allowing the job to make forward progress.
Would asynchronous prefetch mean reclamation is invisible to training?

Not necessarily. “Asynchronous” characterizes how prefetch is initiated relative to other work; it is not a promise that training never waits or that offload has no performance effect. The stated training requirement is forward progress through reclamation without restarting or optimizer-state corruption, rather than zero observable delay.
Can you distinguish what each part contributes without claiming they guarantee the result?

Latency-profiled admission addresses which mixed workloads the runtime accepts. Bounded training kernel slices create recurring opportunities to choose what runs, and inference-priority dispatch gives inference preference at those choices. Versioned optimizer-state offload and asynchronous prefetch at step boundaries address reclaiming memory from stateful training while preserving a path for training to continue. Those are complementary design elements; their combination still needs to satisfy both the inference p99 bound and the training-continuity requirement.
So should I describe this as an implementation with a proven latency bound?

Describe it as a proposal for the runtime, not as a completed implementation or proven result. Its intended target remains inference p99 within 1.2× the isolated baseline under admitted mixed workloads, alongside training forward progress through memory reclamation without restarting or corrupting optimizer state.
What if I only mention priority dispatch and offload when I present the proposal?

That would omit two explicit parts of the proposed combination. Latency-profiled admission matters to the scope of the mixed workloads, and bounded training kernel slices matter to when dispatch can give inference preference. The full proposal also includes inference-priority dispatch and versioned optimizer-state offload with asynchronous prefetch at step boundaries.
What kernel-slice duration and optimizer-state offload bandwidth would keep inference p99 at or below 1.2× its isolated baseline without stalling training?

That is the key sizing question for the proposal, but the information so far does not determine either number. We need a combination of slice duration and offload bandwidth that satisfies both conditions under the admitted mixed workloads: the inference p99 bound and training that does not stall. The proposal names the mechanisms, not their required settings.
Why do those two quantities need to be considered together?

Kernel-slice duration affects how long training work can run before inference-priority dispatch has another opportunity to favor inference. Optimizer-state offload bandwidth affects how quickly state can be moved for memory reclamation while training continues. A setting that looks acceptable for inference in isolation from the memory question could still leave training waiting for state; sufficient offload bandwidth alone would not establish the inference p99 bound.
Is 1.2× the target duration for a training slice?

No. The 1.2× figure is a limit on inference p99 latency relative to its isolated baseline, under admitted mixed workloads. It is not a slice duration or an offload-bandwidth value. The question is which duration and bandwidth, if any, allow that latency condition to hold without stalling training.
Would choosing the shortest possible slices settle the inference side?

Not from the information given. Shorter slices could create more frequent opportunities for inference-priority dispatch, but the p99 requirement concerns observed inference latency under admitted mixed workloads. No numerical relationship between slice duration and that p99 has been established here, so a slice duration cannot be selected just from the 1.2× limit.
Could we at least state a minimum optimizer-state offload bandwidth?

Not numerically. The question does not supply the amount of optimizer state to offload or the time available to move it without stalling training. Offload is also paired in the proposal with asynchronous prefetch at step boundaries, so merely naming an offload bandwidth would not, on its own, establish that the needed state is available when training continues.
Does “without stalling training” just mean the job eventually makes forward progress?

The question asks specifically whether the chosen settings avoid stalling training; it should not be silently weakened to eventual forward progress. The broader runtime requirement also says training must maintain forward progress through reclamation without restarting or corrupting optimizer state. The sizing question asks whether latency can be protected while avoiding a training stall, not whether a restart or state corruption would be an acceptable workaround.
Should I look for one best slice duration first, then choose bandwidth afterward?

The question does not establish that there is a single best duration or that the two values can be chosen independently. It asks for a duration-and-bandwidth combination that meets the inference p99 limit without stalling training. Considering them jointly keeps both constraints visible, without assuming a particular answer.
What would count as an answer to the question, then?

An answer would identify a kernel-slice duration and an optimizer-state offload bandwidth, with a basis for saying that, under the admitted mixed workloads, inference p99 is no more than 1.2× its isolated baseline and training does not stall. Those values have not been supplied or established in this discussion.

I have a hypothesis for the sizing question: at kernel slices of ≤1 ms and optimizer-state offload bandwidth of ≥12 GB/s, inference p99 stays ≤1.2× its isolated baseline, and training advances with intact optimizer state.

That gives the proposal a concrete hypothesis to assess. It pairs a maximum kernel-slice duration of 1 ms with a minimum optimizer-state offload bandwidth of 12 GB/s, and predicts both the inference p99 bound and continued training with intact optimizer state. It is a hypothesis, not an established performance or correctness result.
Do the inequalities include exactly 1 ms and exactly 12 GB/s?

Yes. “≤1 ms” includes a 1 ms kernel slice, and “≥12 GB/s” includes 12 GB/s of optimizer-state offload bandwidth. The hypothesis is about the combination of those conditions, rather than about either number alone.
Is the 1.2× figure still a comparison to inference running alone?

Yes. The prediction is that inference p99 under the admitted mixed workload stays no greater than 1.2 times its isolated baseline. It is a relative latency bound, not an absolute latency in milliseconds; the 1 ms value refers to kernel-slice duration.
So are you saying that ≤1 ms slices by themselves guarantee the latency target?
No. The hypothesis pairs ≤1 ms slices with ≥12 GB/s optimizer-state offload. It does not establish that the slice limit alone guarantees the p99 result, nor does it report a test of that claim.
Could ≥12 GB/s offload alone be enough, regardless of the slice duration?

That is not what this hypothesis says either. The predicted outcome is attached to both thresholds together. It does not claim that offload bandwidth alone controls inference p99, or that arbitrary training kernel slices would be acceptable.
What does “training advances with intact optimizer state” add to the latency prediction?

It makes training behavior part of the predicted outcome. The hypothesis is not satisfied merely because inference p99 meets its bound: training must also keep advancing, and its optimizer state must remain intact as memory is reclaimed. Those properties matter because the jobs are stateful.
Does “advances” mean training can never wait for offload or prefetch?

Not necessarily. The hypothesis says training advances with intact optimizer state; it does not explicitly assert that there is never a wait. The sizing question asks about avoiding a training stall, so that aspect would need to be assessed rather than assumed from the word “advances.”
Could I report these thresholds as measured operating limits?
No. They are proposed thresholds in a hypothesis. Nothing here reports measurements showing that ≤1 ms slices and ≥12 GB/s offload achieve the predicted inference p99 or training behavior.
If a workload used 0.8 ms slices and 14 GB/s offload, would the hypothesis cover that combination?

Numerically, 0.8 ms satisfies ≤1 ms, and 14 GB/s satisfies ≥12 GB/s. The hypothesis would therefore predict its stated outcomes for that combination within its workload scope. That is not confirmation that the outcomes would actually occur.
What if the slices were longer than 1 ms, or offload bandwidth were below 12 GB/s?

Those combinations fall outside at least one stated condition. The hypothesis does not tell us whether inference p99 would pass or fail there, or whether training would advance with intact optimizer state. Its thresholds define where the prediction applies; they are not claims that all other settings fail.
Is 12 GB/s meant to specify an offload destination or a particular way to measure bandwidth?

No destination or bandwidth-measurement convention is specified in the hypothesis. It names optimizer-state offload bandwidth and sets a ≥12 GB/s threshold. A more detailed assessment would need to make the bandwidth meaning clear, but we should not supply a device, transfer path, or measurement definition that has not been stated.
Can I infer from “intact optimizer state” that the offload and prefetch protocol is already correct?

No. Intact optimizer state is an outcome the hypothesis predicts, not proof of a correct protocol. The proposal involves versioned optimizer-state offload and asynchronous prefetch at step boundaries, but the hypothesis does not provide an implementation or a correctness demonstration.
How would you phrase the claim so the uncertainty remains obvious?

“We hypothesize that, with training kernel slices of ≤1 ms and optimizer-state offload bandwidth of ≥12 GB/s, inference p99 under admitted mixed workloads remains ≤1.2× its isolated baseline while training advances with intact optimizer state.” That retains both thresholds and both predicted outcomes without presenting them as observed results.
Does the hypothesis settle whether this is the best slice-and-bandwidth combination?

No. It proposes a combination expected to meet the stated outcomes; it does not establish optimality, compare alternatives, or say the thresholds are necessary. The specific question it puts on the table is whether the predicted latency and training behavior hold at settings satisfying both inequalities.
How should we evaluate the hypothesis about ≤1 ms kernel slices and ≥12 GB/s optimizer-state offload?

Run H100 MixBench, sweeping kernel-slice durations from 0.5–2 ms and optimizer-state offload bandwidth from 8–16 GB/s. For the settings examined, measure inference p99 against its isolated baseline, record training steps, and check optimizer-state checksums. That activity is intended to evaluate the hypothesis; it does not yet report an outcome.
Why sweep ranges instead of testing only 1 ms and 12 GB/s?

The ranges let the evaluation examine settings around and across the proposed thresholds, rather than only one combination. The 0.5–2 ms slice range spans the ≤1 ms condition, and the 8–16 GB/s offload range spans the ≥12 GB/s condition. The activity does not specify increments, a complete set of combinations, or a result for any setting.
Would a 2 ms slice be a test of the hypothesis itself?

A 2 ms slice is within the planned sweep but outside the hypothesis’s ≤1 ms condition. Observing it could help characterize the sweep, but the hypothesis does not predict that a 2 ms setting must pass or fail. To assess its stated prediction directly, we would look at examined settings that satisfy both ≤1 ms slices and ≥12 GB/s offload.
And an 8 GB/s offload setting?

That is within the planned 8–16 GB/s sweep but below the hypothesis’s ≥12 GB/s condition. It should not be treated as a setting the hypothesis claims will meet its outcomes. The proposed activity includes it without supplying a prediction for it.
What exactly is the inference measurement meant to answer?

It asks whether inference p99 at a swept mixed-workload setting is no more than 1.2× the isolated inference baseline. Measuring p99 *versus baseline* retains the comparison in the goal and hypothesis; reporting p99 without that comparison would not, by itself, answer the stated latency question.
Does the 0.5–2 ms range say anything about the inference baseline’s duration?
No. Those numbers are training kernel-slice durations. The inference baseline is the reference for the p99 latency comparison, not a value specified by the slice-duration sweep.
Why record training steps as well as inference latency?

The runtime is not supposed to protect inference by preventing training from advancing. Recording training steps provides an observation of training progress alongside the p99 measurement. A latency result alone would leave the training side of the hypothesis unaddressed.
If training records some steps, does that prove it never stalls during reclamation?

Not by itself. A step count can show advancement over an observation, but a nonzero count alone does not establish that no waiting or temporary stall occurred. The activity specifies measuring training steps; it does not define a separate stall measurement or claim that the steps already demonstrate stall-free operation.
What are optimizer checksums for in this activity?

They are an integrity check on optimizer state while assessing whether training advances under memory reclamation. The hypothesis predicts intact optimizer state, so observing training steps without checking state would miss an important part of it. The activity names optimizer checksums as a measurement, but does not specify a checksum method or report any checksum results.
Would a checksum alone prove every aspect of optimizer-state correctness?

No. Checksums are a way to check the state, not a blanket proof of every correctness property. The proposed activity is to measure optimizer checksums alongside training steps and inference p99; it does not claim that those observations have already established correctness.
Should we report a passing result now because the sweep covers the hypothesized thresholds?

No. Covering those thresholds in a planned sweep is not the same as observing the predicted outcomes. H100 MixBench still needs to be run, and the p99-versus-baseline, training-step, and optimizer-checksum measurements still need to be assessed.
Would it be enough to find one setting in the sweep where inference p99 is within 1.2× baseline?

That would address only the inference measurement for that setting. The hypothesis also predicts training advancement with intact optimizer state at settings meeting both thresholds. The evaluation therefore needs the training-step and optimizer-checksum observations for the settings it assesses, without assuming an inference pass establishes the training outcome.
How should I describe the H100 MixBench work in a status update?

You could say: “Plan to run H100 MixBench across 0.5–2 ms kernel slices and 8–16 GB/s optimizer-state offload bandwidth, measuring inference p99 against its isolated baseline, training steps, and optimizer checksums to evaluate the ≤1 ms and ≥12 GB/s hypothesis.” That describes the activity and its purpose without implying that measurements have been collected.
So the sweep might also tell us what happens outside the hypothesized range, even though the hypothesis does not predict it?

Yes. The proposed sweep includes slice durations above 1 ms and offload bandwidth below 12 GB/s. Measurements there could describe those examined settings, but they should not be read as outcomes the hypothesis itself promised. The central test remains whether its predicted latency and training behavior hold for examined settings satisfying both stated thresholds.
What did H100 MixBench report at 1 ms kernel slices and 12 GB/s optimizer-state offload?
At that setting, inference p99 was 1.16× its isolated baseline. The run recorded 2,400 training steps, and the optimizer checksums matched the reference.
When you say 1.16×, is that an absolute latency?
No. It is a ratio: the measured inference p99 was 1.16 times the isolated inference p99. The evidence does not give either p99 as an absolute time.
Can I describe that as a 16% increase relative to the isolated baseline?
Yes. A ratio of 1.16× expresses a p99 value 16% higher than the isolated baseline. That is another way to state the reported measurement, not an additional measurement.
Do the 2,400 steps tell us how long the run lasted?
No. They are a count of training steps recorded in H100 MixBench. The evidence does not specify elapsed time or a steps-per-second rate.
What does it mean that the optimizer checksums matched the reference?

It means the optimizer-state checksum results reported for this run agreed with the reference checksums used for comparison. The evidence does not describe how those checksums or the reference were produced.
Is a reference-matching checksum the same as a complete proof about optimizer state?

No. It is a reported integrity observation for the checked state in this run. The evidence does not claim that a checksum establishes every property of optimizer state or every possible behavior during reclamation.
Should I say that training never had to wait during those 2,400 steps?

The reported step count does not establish that. It says 2,400 steps were recorded, but gives no account of whether training waited at any point. It is best to keep the step count separate from claims about uninterrupted execution.
Are the 1 ms and 12 GB/s figures averages across the sweep?

They identify the setting associated with these reported measurements: 1 ms kernel slices and 12 GB/s offload. This evidence does not provide an average across settings or results for other points in the planned sweep.
Can I infer what happened at 0.5 ms slices or 16 GB/s offload?

Not from this evidence. Although those values were within the planned sweep ranges, the reported result here is specifically for 1 ms slices and 12 GB/s offload. No measurements for those other settings are stated.
Does the result say where the optimizer state was offloaded?
No. It reports the offload bandwidth setting and the reference-matching optimizer checksums, but not an offload destination or transfer path.
What is the most precise way to quote the result without filling in anything missing?

“In H100 MixBench at 1 ms kernel slices and 12 GB/s optimizer-state offload, inference p99 was 1.16× its isolated baseline; the run recorded 2,400 training steps, and optimizer checksums matched the reference.”
What setting should we adopt for the GPU-sharing runtime?

Adopt 1 ms training kernel slices and a 12 GB/s optimizer-state offload reservation for admitted MixBench-class workloads. The decision is based on measured latency and optimizer integrity meeting the requirements for that scope.
Is the 12 GB/s figure a reservation, rather than just an offload rate we happened to observe?
Yes. In this decision, 12 GB/s is the offload reservation to adopt. The decision does not specify how the runtime enforces that reservation or how it divides it among training jobs.
Does “1 ms slices” mean we are adopting the whole range of slice durations that was considered?
No. The adopted setting is 1 ms slices. This decision does not select other slice durations or make a claim about how they would perform.
What exactly limits where we use these settings?

The decision applies to **admitted MixBench-class workloads**. Both qualifications matter: it does not extend the adoption to workloads outside that class, and it does not say that every MixBench-class workload must be admitted. It also does not define the admission rule or the boundaries of the class.
Can I say measured inference latency meets the 1.2× isolated-baseline requirement in that scope?

Yes. Measured latency meeting the requirement is an explicit reason for the decision. The latency requirement is inference p99 within 1.2× its isolated baseline under admitted mixed workloads; the decision applies that measured conclusion to the admitted MixBench-class scope, not to arbitrary workloads.
And what does the optimizer-integrity part of the decision establish?

The decision states that measured optimizer integrity meets the requirement for the adopted scope. That matters because memory reclamation must not corrupt the stateful training jobs’ optimizer state. It is not a claim that every possible optimizer-state behavior or workload has been covered.
Does the decision also say training was proven never to stall?

No. Its stated basis is measured latency and optimizer integrity, and it adopts the settings for the specified workloads. It does not separately state that training never waited or establish a stall-free guarantee. We should not add that conclusion to the decision.
Would it be accurate to call 1 ms and 12 GB/s universal thresholds for the runtime?

No. They are the slice setting and offload reservation adopted for admitted MixBench-class workloads. The decision does not say they are necessary, optimal, or sufficient for every workload the runtime could encounter.
How would you state the decision succinctly without overstating it?

“For admitted MixBench-class workloads, adopt 1 ms training kernel slices and a 12 GB/s optimizer-state offload reservation; measured latency and optimizer integrity meet the requirements in that scope.”
What is the implementation plan for the GPU-sharing runtime?

Implement profile-based admission, 1 ms training kernel slices, and versioned optimizer-state offload and prefetch with a 12 GB/s offload provision. Add release gates for inference p99, training progress, and optimizer checksums. This is a plan for implementation and release checks, not a statement that the implementation has been completed.
How does profile-based admission fit with the fixed 1 ms slice setting?

They address different parts of the plan. Profile-based admission determines which mixed workloads the runtime accepts; 1 ms slices are the planned training execution setting for the adopted scope of admitted MixBench-class workloads. The plan does not specify a profiling procedure or an admission formula.
Does implementing admission mean promising the inference bound for any workload that arrives?

No. The inference requirement is scoped to admitted mixed workloads. Profile-based admission is how the plan makes that scope operational, but it does not extend the ≤1.2× isolated-baseline p99 requirement to arbitrary workloads that have not been admitted.
What should I understand by “1 ms slices” in the plan?

It names the planned duration for training kernel slices. It is not an inference-latency value: inference p99 is assessed separately against its isolated baseline. The plan does not give further rules for forming or dispatching those slices.
Is 12 GB/s an inference bandwidth target?

No. It belongs to the planned optimizer-state offload and prefetch work, not to inference latency. The adopted setting calls for a 12 GB/s offload reservation. The plan does not state a separate numerical prefetch-bandwidth requirement or explain how the reservation will be enforced.
Why does the plan say “versioned” optimizer offload and prefetch?

The training jobs are stateful, and their optimizer state must remain intact through memory reclamation. Versioning is part of the planned offload and prefetch approach for keeping track of the state training needs as it advances. The plan does not spell out a complete versioning protocol, so the word alone should not be treated as a correctness guarantee.
Does this plan change the requirement that training continue without restarting?

No. Implementation of offload and prefetch must still support training forward progress through memory reclamation without restarting or corrupting optimizer state. The release checks in the plan are there to assess progress and integrity; they do not relax either requirement.
What is a release gate here?

It is a check to apply before releasing the runtime. The plan calls for three kinds: an inference-p99 gate, a training-progress gate, and an optimizer-checksum gate. It does not specify the release process, test duration, or a complete pass/fail procedure for those gates.
What comparison should the p99 release gate make?

It should address the stated latency requirement: for admitted mixed workloads, inference p99 must stay within 1.2× its isolated baseline. The plan names a p99 release gate, but it does not provide a new numerical threshold or change the baseline comparison.
Would passing the p99 gate alone be enough to release?

Not under this plan. It also calls for training-progress and optimizer-checksum release gates. Protecting inference p99 cannot substitute for checking that training continues through reclamation and that optimizer state remains intact.
What does the training-progress gate need to guard against?

It needs to address the requirement that training maintain forward progress while memory is reclaimed, rather than being left unable to advance or being restarted as a workaround. The plan does not prescribe a numerical progress rate or a particular way to measure it.
And the checksum gate is about state integrity rather than speed?

Yes. Optimizer checksums are the planned release check directed at optimizer-state integrity. They complement the training-progress gate: advancing steps would not excuse corrupted state, and intact state alone would not show that training continues to advance. The plan does not specify the checksum algorithm or reference procedure.
Can we say the release gates have already passed because these settings were adopted?

No. Adopting settings and planning release gates are different actions. This node calls for implementing the runtime and applying those checks; it does not report that the implementation is finished or that any release gate has passed.
Should the plan include results for every slice duration and offload bandwidth that was considered?

That is not part of this implementation plan. It selects 1 ms slices and the 12 GB/s offload provision, then calls for release gates covering p99, training progress, and optimizer checksums. It does not specify implementing multiple slice or bandwidth settings.
Can you state the plan without making the gates sound like an afterthought?

Implement profile-based admission, 1 ms training kernel slices, and versioned optimizer-state offload and prefetch with a 12 GB/s offload reservation; make inference p99, training progress, and optimizer checksums release gates. The gates keep both sides of the goal visible: bounded inference latency under admitted mixed workloads and training that continues through memory reclamation without restarting or corrupting optimizer state.
For the next implementation activity, what exactly goes into ShareRun v0.1?

Implement versioned optimizer-state eviction and prefetch at step boundaries in ShareRun v0.1, reserve 12 GB/s for the offload work, and verify checksums of restored tensors. That states the implementation activity; it does not say the feature is already complete or that verification has passed.
What is meant by optimizer-state eviction here?

It is the part of the activity concerned with removing optimizer state from the GPU memory being reclaimed while preserving a way to restore the state training needs. The activity names versioned eviction, but it does not specify the destination, the representation of the evicted state, or which tensors are selected.
Is prefetch a separate feature, or part of the same activity?

It is part of the same activity. ShareRun v0.1 is to implement both eviction and prefetch of versioned optimizer state at step boundaries. Eviction addresses making memory available; prefetch addresses bringing state back for continued use. Neither operation should be described as implemented merely because it is listed here.
Does “at step boundaries” apply to both eviction and prefetch?
Yes. The activity places versioned optimizer-state eviction and prefetch at step boundaries. It does not specify a more precise point within a boundary or an ordering for individual tensors.
Why keep versions if the state is going to be restored anyway?

Versioning distinguishes optimizer-state instances as training advances, so eviction and restoration can refer to the intended state. It is a named part of the implementation activity, not by itself proof that restored data will be correct; verifying restored tensor checksums is also explicitly required.
What does the 12 GB/s number commit this activity to?

It calls for reserving 12 GB/s for the optimizer-state offload work in ShareRun v0.1. It is a bandwidth reservation in the activity, not a reported achieved transfer rate. The activity does not say how that reservation is enforced or provide a separate numeric prefetch-bandwidth reservation.
Can I interpret 12 GB/s as the size of the optimizer state?
No. GB/s is a bandwidth unit: gigabytes per second. The activity specifies a 12 GB/s reservation, not the amount of optimizer state or the time required to evict or prefetch it.
What exactly gets checked after prefetch?

The checksums of restored tensors are to be verified. That directs the check at the tensor contents after restoration, rather than treating a completed transfer alone as evidence that the restored contents are right.
